rules.quote: Remove any adverb that doesn’t play a critical function in a sentence.
rules.specification: The page does not define what makes an adverb’s function critical. It also provides no frequency threshold for ‘sparingly’ or ‘occasionally’.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence contains an adverb that does not play a critical function.
rules.why: G-4: the occasional-use and sparing-use instructions are consolidated into the more specific instruction about unnecessary adverbs.

covers.quote: In general, you simply add the word ‘more’ or ‘most’ in front of the adverb.
Not all adverbs follow this regular pattern of using ‘more’ or ‘most’ to show comparison.

parts.quote: Bob spoke more quickly than Tom.
Tom speaks more quickly than Bob, but Harry speaks the most quickly of them all.
He spoke well, but she spoke better.
You finished work early, but they finished even earlier.

rules.quote: Make sure you use the correct form.
rules.specification: Read ‘correct form’ in the context of this comparison section: distinguish comparative and superlative adverb forms from adjective forms. The regular ‘more’/‘most’ construction is not a requirement for irregular adverbs.
rules.violation_condition: A comparative or superlative adjective form is used where an adverb form is required, such as ‘quickest’ instead of ‘most quickly’.
when: Applies when an adverb expresses comparative or superlative degree.
Irregular comparative forms, such as ‘better’ and ‘earlier’, do not require ‘more’.
rules.why: G-4: the body supplies the instruction beneath a descriptive heading. G-2: regular and irregular comparison forms are cases of the same correct-form check.
